title: 19 · Built-in architecture, runtime tuning and deliberate distributed design

paras: A refinement of the previous chapter: distinguish capabilities supplied by silicon and operating systems, tunable behavior on one machine, and architectures requiring multi-system coordination.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook

blocks.h2: Three decision layers—not three absolute categories
paras: Layer A · Platform-provided foundations. CPU ISA and cores, caches, address translation support, firmware and the operating system's memory manager are supplied by the chosen platform. They do not require inventing an architecture from scratch, but the choice of processor, kernel, machine type and deployment still matters. Virtual memory and paging are typically enabled and managed by the OS; segmentation varies greatly by ISA and OS. UMA is not universal : some servers expose NUMA topology.

Layer B · Configurable runtime behavior. Thread placement, CPU affinity, NUMA policy, huge pages, swap policy, cache-aware algorithms, concurrency limits and workload scheduling may require deliberate tuning. Shared-memory concurrency is not automatically safe: synchronization and memory ordering still matter. Cache hardware is automatic; cache-friendly software design is not.

Layer C · Architectures that must be composed. Client–server, peer-to-peer, microservices, clusters, distributed storage, distributed memory abstractions, load balancing and autoscaling require explicit design, deployment, networking, security, failure handling and operations. Some cloud services automate parts of this, but automation does not remove architectural choices.

Edge meanings: hardware provides execution and devices to the OS; the OS exposes managed resources to applications; runtime policy changes resource use; application components communicate locally or over networks; distributed deployment adds inter-node failures, coordination and security boundaries.

blocks.h2: Technical accuracy notes (editorial, not alterations to originals)
paras: RISC and CISC are ISA design families, not automatic versus manually designed architectures. SIMD is an instruction/data parallelism model and does not imply a super-scalar processor; superscalar means issuing multiple instructions per cycle. MIMD can exist inside one multiprocessor machine as well as across machines. MPP often describes large-scale parallel systems, not necessarily shared memory. NGINX and HAProxy can distribute application traffic; cloud ELB is a managed load-balancing family, and Kubernetes autoscaling is a separate resource-control mechanism. These are complementary layers, not interchangeable alternatives.
